Independent transformations, isomorphism criterion and examples

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: A formal framework relates design languages by transforming the grammars that generate them.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: What should change—and what should remain connected—when one grammar becomes another?

sections.title: Main idea
sections.text: A normal form separates spatial composition from control of rule application. Their independent changes can preserve a meaningful structural relationship.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Specify labeled shapes and spatial relations, attach state-label pairs to addition/subtraction rules, then define a recursive dependency relation from selected derivations.

sections.title: Worked evidence
sections.text: One grammar develops into sixteen transformed examples. Directed graphs show the preserved recursive structure; redundant copies of rules permit multiple changed versions of one original rule.

sections.title: Formal outcome
sections.text: Shape-change and state-change transformations commute because they act on separate components. Isomorphic recursive structures constrain transformations and transfer understanding of rule dependencies.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: Recursive structure depends on a finite catalogue of chosen derivations. Different understandings of a language can therefore produce different dependency relations; the normal form need not be concise.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Labels can govern where or how rules apply, while state labels govern when. Grammar transformation must consider both geometry and control.

terms.meaning: Here, a dependency relation between rules and the initial shape, defined relative to selected derivations.
A nonspatial control indicating which stage or state permits a rule application.
